nameStory: The 'resinous' in this polypore's name comes from its distinctly aromatic, resin-like smell that's reminiscent of pine pitch or benzoin (a fragrant tree resin). When you encounter this bracket fungus, that sweet, medicinal fragrance is often your first clue to its identity. It's also called the 'late fall polypore' because it typically appears when most other mushrooms have finished their season.
description: The Resinous Polypore is a bracket fungus that grows like a shelf from the sides of dead hardwood trees, particularly favoring birch and beech. Its semicircular caps can reach 6-12 inches across and have a distinctive reddish-brown to dark brown color when fresh. Unlike gilled mushrooms, it has tiny pores on its underside instead of gills. The fungus has a thick, sturdy texture and that characteristic resinous aroma that sets it apart from other bracket fungi.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Has a strong, sweet, resinous fragrance similar to pine pitch, benzoin, or medicinal ointment - this aromatic quality is your best identification feature

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Semicircular bracket shape, reddish-brown to dark brown when fresh, becoming darker with age; surface is smooth to slightly bumpy and can feel sticky when moist

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Underside has tiny, round pores (not gills) that are white when young, becoming yellowish-brown with age; pores bruise brown when pressed

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels firm and somewhat rubbery when fresh, becoming hard and woody as it ages; younger specimens can be cut with a knife

idTips.label: Attachment
idTips.description: Grows directly from tree trunks without a stem, forming shelf-like brackets that can overlap in groups

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: Fresh specimens may exude a reddish-brown liquid when cut or damaged, and the cut surface darkens over time

habitat: Look for Resinous Polypore on dead or dying hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, with a strong preference for birch and beech trees. It's commonly found in mixed deciduous and coniferous forests from sea level to mountainous areas. The fungus acts as a decomposer, breaking down dead wood, so check fallen logs and dead standing trees in both mature forests and woodland edges.

seasonality.spring: Old specimens from previous years may still be visible but are usually dark, hard, and less aromatic. New growth is just beginning on suitable dead wood.
seasonality.summer: Fresh fruiting bodies start to appear in mid to late summer, showing their characteristic reddish-brown colors and strong resinous scent.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for fresh, aromatic specimens - this is when you'll find the best examples with their full fragrance and softer texture.
seasonality.winter: Older brackets persist through winter but become hard, dark, and lose much of their distinctive smell, though they remain identifiable by shape and habitat.

funFact: The Resinous Polypore's distinctive smell comes from compounds similar to those found in benzoin resin, which has been used in perfumes and incense for over 500 years - you're essentially smelling the same aromatic molecules that ancient traders carried along spice routes!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other dark bracket fungi like Chaga or Artist's Conk, but the Resinous Polypore's sweet, medicinal smell is unmistakable once you know it. Memory trick: 'Resinous = aromatic' - if it doesn't have that distinctive pine-pitch fragrance, it's not a Resinous Polypore.
contextualKnowledge: This species is sometimes called 'Benzoin Bracket' in field guides, which can be confusing since there's actually a separate species called Ischnoderma benzoinum (also called Benzoin Bracket). Both have similar resinous scents, leading to naming overlap in popular literature.
compareHints: The closely related Benzoin Bracket (Ischnoderma benzoinum) is very similar but tends to be lighter in color and may have a slightly different aromatic profile. Both species share that characteristic resinous smell and bracket growth form, making them difficult to distinguish without microscopic examination. In the field, Resinous Polypore is generally darker and more common in New England forests.
